decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what a presentation is: the form and why it is used. Second, planning and structuring a presentation: how one is put together, from the brief to a clear shape. Third, designing visual aids and avoiding common errors: making slides that help rather than hinder. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about academic presentations: what they are and how one is put together. By the end you will be able to explain what an academic presentation is and why it is used, describe how a presentation is planned and structured, and identify effective visual aids and the common errors to avoid.

These are not abstract skills. Presentations are a common form of assessment across subjects, and they build the communication skills that employers look for. Knowing what a presentation is, and how to build one, changes how you prepare and the marks your work earns.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain what a presentation is, describe how one is planned and structured, identify effective visual aids and common errors.

practiceConnection.academic: Presenting is a skill academic study asks of you again and again. Seminars, poster sessions, group projects and vivas all ask you to speak to an audience and make a point clearly. The same skill is prized at work, where employers value graduates who can communicate well. Build the foundations now and they carry into every module of your degree, and into professional life beyond it.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced presenting courses take you into delivering a presentation well across different formats, and into presenting with authority and collaborating in group work. Going wider: the same foundations underpin Academic Writing, Reflective Practice and Work-Based and Experiential Learning, where you put communication to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. A presentation is no longer a daunting unknown: it is a form of work you understand and can prepare for. You can explain what an academic presentation is and why it is used, a spoken argument made to an audience and assessed. You can describe how one is planned and structured, from the brief through to an introduction, main body and conclusion. And you can identify effective visual aids and the common errors to avoid. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, presenting is something you practise in many modules. Each seminar talk, each poster, each group presentation puts these foundations to work. It is also what professional life rewards: the ability to communicate an idea clearly to an audience travels well beyond your degree, and is among the skills employers ask for most.
